title: A Stoic birthday
hookLine: Seneca would ask: how much of this past year did you really live?

cards: Candles on a cake. Someone counts them, or gives up and uses a number-shaped candle instead. Thirty-four.
Fifty-two. Seventy-one. Everyone sings, slightly off key, and somebody says: another year older!

The number is the headline of a birthday. But Seneca, who wrote a whole essay about how we spend our time, would lean across the table, very politely, and ask a different question. Not how many years.
How much of this past year did you actually live?

teach.h: LIFE IS LONG, IF YOU USE IT.
teach.b: First, the essay. Seneca's On the Shortness of Life, written to a friend named Paulinus, opens with a complaint everyone makes: life is too short. Seneca disagrees.
Life is long enough, he says, if we use it well. It's we who make it short, by wasting it. Second, the audit.
Imagine an old man, he says, and add up his years honestly. How many went to a demanding boss, to quarrels, to errands around the city, to worries he invented, to things he didn't even enjoy?
Take those away, and he has far fewer years than he counts. Third, the sharpest line. Don't think someone has lived long because of gray hair and wrinkles.
That person hasn't lived long; they've been around long. It's like a sailor caught in a storm the moment he leaves the harbor, blown in circles for days. He didn't have a long voyage.
He was just tossed about a lot. Fourth, a birthday on the porch. Seneca isn't asking for guilt.
He's asking for an honest count.
Which days this past year were actually lived, with attention, with people, with something that mattered? Those count. The others aren't failures; they're information.
A birthday is a good day to ask, because the next year hasn't been spent yet.

how: Some readers of Seneca use a birthday or new year to review how much of the past year they truly lived, and what they want more of in the next.

o: a Stoic teacher who wrote a book on old age
the friend Seneca wrote to on the shortness of life
the Roman emperor who sent Seneca into exile

games.q: how much did I live — tap the pairs.
p: not proof of a long life

s: Seneca agrees that life is too short
he says life is long enough if used well; we make it short by wasting it.
Seneca compares a long but wasted life to a sailor tossed by a storm
he didn't voyage far; he was just tossed about.
Seneca's point is to make you feel guilty about wasted time
he asks for an honest count, so the next year can be lived.

games.q: it's your birthday. Seneca joins the party. what does he ask?
o: how much of this year did you really live?
games.why: for Seneca, years counted aren't the same as years lived; the honest count is the gift.

practice: Whether it's your birthday or not, look back over the last twelve months and find three moments when you were fully alive, present with people or work or a place that mattered, and let them count.
Then gently notice one stretch that slipped away, scrolling, worrying, rushing, with no blame. Ask what you'd want more of, and less of, in the year ahead.

wordCard.voice: Paulinus, the friend to whom Seneca addressed his essay asking not how many years we've had, but how much of them we've truly lived. Today's word.

orig.s: non ille diu vixit, sed diu fuit
orig.say: nohn IL-leh DEE-oo VIK-sit, sed DEE-oo FOO-it
orig.note: Latin, On the Shortness of Life 7: he has not lived long, he has existed long.

carryVoice: Your line: how much did I live. Lived long, or only around long. That's day six hundred seventy-four.

sources.work: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae)
